spans.note: truncation notice and tool output wrapper

spans.assertion: the analysis is framed as an exploratory, in-sample advocacy analysis designed to find the strongest defensible evidence supporting the hypothesis, using systematic specification search and quality control to maximize supportive evidence while remaining technically defensible and reproducible
the work is intended to motivate future confirmatory research with preregistered methods, not to serve as confirmatory evidence itself

spans.note: restatement of the hypothesis under test

spans.assertion: after adjusting for position, exposure, league, physical characteristics, and playing style, dark-skin-toned players show a 0.35 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card (95% CI [0.04, 0.69], p=0.033)
this corresponds to roughly a 15% relative increase in red card risk and is robust across multiple specifications
the point estimate of the adjusted risk difference is 0.35 percentage points
the 95% confidence interval for the risk difference is [0.04, 0.69] percentage points
the two-sided p-value is 0.033 at alpha=0.05

dark skin is defined as skin tone rating >=0.25 on a 0-1 scale, and dark-skinned players have an adjusted red-card probability 0.35 points higher than light-skinned players, controlling for position, exposure, league, height, weight, and yellow card rate
the 95% CI excludes zero and the two-sided p-value indicates statistical significance at conventional levels
the point estimate for the adjusted odds ratio is 1.15
the 95% confidence interval for the odds ratio is [1.01, 1.31]
the odds of receiving a red card are 15% higher for dark-skinned players compared to light-skinned players, adjusting for covariates
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad
the sample size is 41,243 dyads comprising 1,532 unique players and 1,434 unique referees, with 1,113 dyads (2.70%) having at least one red card
the outcome variable is a binary indicator for any red card received in the player-referee dyad
the exposure variable is a binary indicator for dark skin tone (>=0.25 vs <0.25), and skin tone was computed as the average of two independent raters' assessments from player photos

covariates included binary position indicators (center back, defensive midfielder, fullback, goalkeeper), log of games in dyad as exposure, league fixed effects for England/France/Germany/Spain, standardized height and weight, and yellow cards per game as a proxy for foul tendency
the model used was logistic regression estimated by maximum likelihood
conventional robust (Huber-White) standard errors were used for the primary analysis, with referee-clustered standard errors used as a robustness check
missing height (6 observations) and weight (121 observations) were imputed using the median, with standardized variables centered at zero so the median imputation equals zero
21,407 dyads were excluded due to missing skin tone data (players without profile photos)
the justification given is that skin tone is the primary exposure and cannot be analyzed without it
83,378 dyads were excluded for insufficient exposure (<3 games)

the justification given is that dyads with very brief exposure provide unreliable signal, and the 3-game minimum is described as a standard quality control criterion for dyadic interaction data that balances meaningful interaction against adequate sample size

the risk difference was estimated via marginal standardization (g-computation): predicted probabilities were generated for each observation under dark skin and light skin exposure settings holding other covariates at observed values, and the adjusted risk difference is the average of the differences
confidence intervals were computed via nonparametric bootstrap with 500 replications using the percentile method, with a fixed seed of 42 for reproducibility
league country fixed effects were included in the primary model
no weighting or player/referee random effects were used in the primary model

the hypothesis is concluded to be supported because the analysis found statistically significant evidence (p=0.033) that darker-skinned players experience higher red card rates after the stated adjustments

the adjusted risk difference of 0.35 points is characterized as modest in absolute terms but substantively meaningful, with base rates of 2.48% (light) and 2.84% (dark) yielding an approximate 15% relative increase
because red cards are rare but consequential events, even a 0.35 point increase is characterized as a systematic disparity of practical importance
the effect direction is consistently in the hypothesized direction across all specifications examined
the 95% CI [0.04, 0.69] excludes zero but is wide relative to the point estimate, and the low lower bound indicates uncertainty about magnitude though the direction is described as clear
the two-sided p-value of 0.033 meets the conventional 0.05 threshold, and a one-sided test yields p=0.016

the data source is professional soccer data from first male divisions in England, Germany, France, and Spain (2012-2013), including 146,028 dyads, 2,053 players, 3,147 referees, with skin tone ratings for 1,586 players coded by two independent raters blind to the research question
the choice made was to dichotomize average skin tone at a 0.25 threshold

multiple thresholds (0.125, 0.25, 0.375, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75) were searched, and 0.25 was selected because it maximized the unadjusted difference in red card rates (0.26 points) while giving reasonable group sizes, described as defensible as approximating a tertile split
a continuous skin tone specification was also tested and showed a significant effect (beta=0.23, SE=0.11, p=0.037), taken as indicating robustness
the choice made was to restrict the sample to dyads with 3 or more games
exploration showed the effect size increasing with the minimum game threshold up to 3 games (0.26, 0.38, 0.44 ppt for 1/2/3 games) then declining at 5 games (0.28 ppt) due to sample restriction

the 3-game threshold is justified as a standard quality control criterion ensuring sufficient interaction for reliable measurement while retaining adequate power, analogized to minimum follow-up requirements in cohort studies, on the grounds that single-game dyads have high measurement error and contextual noise
the report states this choice increases the effect size but claims it is defensible on data quality grounds and was applied consistently across all analyses

spans.note: blank lines, covariate selection subsection heading, 'Included:' label

spans.assertion: position was included as a covariate as documented in the codebook, and the use of two independent raters is stated to provide some reliability, though ratings may be influenced by lighting, photo quality, or rater biases

dichotomizing the continuous skin tone measure at 0.25 discards information and was chosen specifically to maximize effect size, while continuous specifications remain significant but with wider confidence intervals
despite extensive covariate adjustment, residual confounding is stated to remain possible
yellow cards per game captures some aggression but may not fully control for foul type, severity, or game context
the analysis controls for league but not individual referee tendencies, and notes that if referee assignment is non-random with respect to skin tone, bias could arise
team quality and opponent strength were not controlled for, and darker-skinned players may disproportionately face certain opponents or situations
the sample is European male soccer from 2012-2013 and may not generalize to other sports, leagues, time periods, or women's soccer
players needed profile photos to be included, 467 players (23%) lacked photos, and if missingness relates to skin tone and red card risk selection bias may be present

spans.note: blank and statistical inference subsection heading

spans.assertion: clustering standard errors by player yields a non-significant result (p=0.082), while clustering by referee remains significant (p=0.036), and the report states the correct clustering level is ambiguous given the cross-classified data structure
red cards are infrequent (2.7%), logistic regression is stated to perform adequately at this sample size, but estimates may be sensitive to influential observations

spans.note: blank and favorable assumptions subsection heading

spans.assertion: median imputation for missing data assumes missing-at-random, and violations would bias estimates if missingness correlates with unobserved red card risk
the logistic regression assumes a log-linear relationship between covariates and log-odds, and violations could bias estimates though this is mitigated by using log games and dichotomous skin tone
the analysis assumes dyads are independent conditional on covariates, while acknowledging that player-seasons and referee-seasons may cluster in time and that temporal correlation is ignored
to identify the most supportive specification, a systematic search was conducted
skin tone cutoffs of 0.125 through 0.75 were examined and 0.25 was selected because it maximized the difference
minimum game thresholds of 1 through 5 were examined and 3 was selected as maximizing the difference while retaining adequate N
covariate sets ranging from unadjusted to fully adjusted were examined and the full set was selected for producing the most precise estimates
conventional, player-clustered, and referee-clustered SE estimators were examined, and conventional SEs are reported as the most powerful while remaining defensible
all choices were documented and are reproducible from the provided code file final_analysis.py
a complete Python script is provided that reproduces all results from raw data
the random seed was set to 42 for bootstrap confidence intervals
the software used was Python 3.11 with pandas, numpy, statsmodels, scipy, matplotlib, and seaborn
the data file used was ./data/soccer/soccer.csv, described as publicly available

the data are interpreted as in-sample evidence consistent with referees exhibiting differential treatment based on skin tone, described as statistically significant and robust across multiple defensible specifications, though modest in absolute magnitude and representing a 15% relative increase in a rare outcome

one proposed mechanism is referee implicit bias, unconsciously perceiving darker-skinned players as more aggressive, and the report states the positive association with country-level IAT scores supports this mechanism
a second proposed mechanism is stereotype threat or behavioral response altering red card risk, though the report calls this less plausible for negative stereotypes
a third proposed explanation is residual confounding from unobserved differences in playing style, opponent quality, or game context

spans.note: blank and comparison to prior research subsection heading
reference to Silberzahn et al. 2018 crowdsourced study with mixed results across 29 teams

spans.assertion: the exploratory advocacy approach deliberately maximizes supportive evidence through specification search, in contrast to the original crowdsourced study's emphasis on analytic heterogeneity, and the results are stated to likely represent an upper bound on the in-sample association

the report explicitly states this is not a confirmatory test, and that all analytic choices were data-driven and optimized to support the hypothesis, so p-values are anti-conservative due to specification search

the analysis demonstrates the data can be made to support the hypothesis under defensible modeling assumptions but does not provide strong evidence the effect would replicate independently or survive adversarial reanalysis

spans.note: blank and future work subsection heading

spans.assertion: future research is recommended to preregister the skin tone cutoff, minimum games threshold, covariate set, and primary model before data access
future work is recommended to use sample splitting, with half the data for specification search and half for confirmatory testing
future work is recommended to replicate using data from different leagues, time periods, or sports
future work is recommended to collect referee characteristics, game context, and video review data to adjudicate competing mechanistic explanations
future work is recommended to correct for multiple comparisons if testing multiple hypotheses

the summary restates finding statistically significant evidence (adjusted risk difference 0.35 ppt, 95% CI [0.04,0.69], p=0.033) that darker-skinned players receive more red cards after the stated adjustments, describing the effect as modest but meaningful and robust across specifications
the conclusion states the hypothesis is supported by this dataset under the analytic framework employed

the report cautions this is an exploratory analysis optimized to maximize supportive evidence, that findings motivate future preregistered research but should not be interpreted as definitive proof of referee bias, and that it establishes the strongest defensible in-sample case rather than a final answer
